planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in sun to light shade; this species forms neat, non-invasive clumps rather than running rhizomes, so it is easier to place in a mixed border than many of its spreading relatives. CAUTION: the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves when dividing or cutting back stems.

directions: Named for plant collector Tony Schilling, who found it in Nepal, this clump-forming spurge sends up dark-green, willow-like leaves on purple-flushed stems topped in mid to late summer by broad heads of lime-yellow bracts that hold their color for many weeks, later aging to coppery tones in autumn. It is more clump-forming and less wanderingly rhizomatous than many border euphorbias, so it mixes well with perennials without swamping them, and it tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than the typical drought-loving Mediterranean spurges. Cut faded flowering stems back to the base once bracts fade to tidy the plant and encourage fresh foliage. Always wear gloves when handling cut stems, since the sap is an irritant to skin and eyes and mildly toxic if ingested.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this alpine species resents hot, wet summer soil, so good drainage is essential, especially in warmer zones.

directions: A circumboreal alpine and subalpine species found from the mountains of Europe to the Rockies, this anemone sends up deeply cut, fern-like basal foliage and wiry stems topped by clusters of 2 to 8 white, saucer-shaped flowers that, true to the name, resemble small narcissus blooms rather than the typical solitary anemone flower. It is best suited to a rock garden, alpine trough, or well-drained raised bed where its need for sharp drainage and cool roots can be met, and it goes dormant by midsummer in warmer gardens so is often paired with later-emerging companions. Unlike woodland anemones, it prefers an open, sunny site and resents being disturbed once settled, so choose its spot carefully. Protect the crown from standing winter wet, which is far more likely to kill it than cold itself.
